predictions.explanation:
The prediction has a horizon of **~10 years from the recording date of 7 Dec 2024**, i.e., until about **2034**. As of today (30 Nov 2025), fewer than 2 years have elapsed, so it is **too early** to say whether the forecast will prove right or wrong.

Current data show that China already has larger total power generation capacity than the U.S., but not at 4x yet. Various international energy statistics (e.g., from the IEA, U.S. EIA, and other energy data compilers) indicate that in recent years China’s installed power capacity and electricity generation have been on the order of **about 2×** that of the U.S., depending on the year and metric (installed capacity vs. actual generation), but not 4×. However, this only describes the situation **now**, not in 2034.

Because the forecast explicitly concerns the situation around **2034**, and that date has not yet occurred, the truth value of the prediction **cannot be determined at this time**. Therefore the status is **inconclusive (too early)**.

For context, as of late 2025, China's total installed capacity is ~3.7 TW (e.g., [Greenpeace Sep 2025](https://www.greenpeace.org/eastasia/press/68510/)), while the US is ~1.2-1.3 TW (inferred from EIA additions on ~1.2 TW base in 2023 + ~100 GW added 2024-25; [Nasdaq May 2025](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/unpacking-high-stakes-us-china-ai-energy-race) states ~3 TW vs 1 TW). Current ratio ~3x, but outcome by 2034 undetermined. Sources: EIA, Ember, Greenpeace.

predictions.explanation:
As of November 30, 2025, Bitcoin is *significant* but still far from being a “serious threat” to the U.S. dollar’s global role, especially as a reserve currency and primary medium of exchange:

- The U.S. dollar still dominates global foreign‑exchange reserves (around 55–60% of disclosed reserves) and international trade invoicing, vastly ahead of all alternatives including cryptocurrencies.
- Bitcoin remains highly volatile and is used primarily as a speculative asset and, to a lesser extent, as a store of value, not as a large‑scale replacement for dollar usage in trade, credit, or official reserves.
- While some countries (e.g., El Salvador) have adopted or experimented with Bitcoin as legal tender and there is ongoing U.S. policy attention (SEC approvals of spot Bitcoin ETFs, enforcement actions, regulatory debates), these steps have not escalated into the kind of **major policy crisis or structural challenge** to dollar hegemony implied by “serious threat.”

Because Gavin’s prediction is explicitly open‑ended (“at some point … Bitcoin will … be a serious threat”), there is no time bound by which it *must* have come true. We cannot say it is wrong; it simply has not clearly materialized *yet*. Therefore, the correct classification today is **inconclusive (too early to tell)**.

Bitcoin's market cap is ~$1.82T (YCharts, Dec 2025), vs. US M2 ~$22.3T (FRED Oct 2025)—~8% scale, not a serious threat. USD holds ~58% global reserves (Fed 'International Role of the US Dollar – 2025 Edition', down from 71% but dominant). No notable policy reactions to a BTC threat; Trump admin pro-crypto (e.g., positioning US as 'crypto capital' per Baker Law, Jan 2025), not defensive of USD. Speculative discussions exist (e.g., Larry Fink letter, Apr 2025), but BTC not yet competitive as store of value/medium of exchange vs. USD.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction explicitly uses a long horizon: *"over the coming years/decades"* for 7–10 new major defense primes, naming Anduril as “obvious” and Saronic and Epirus as likely. Less than one year has passed since the Dec 7, 2024 release date, so the stated time frame has barely begun.

As of Nov 30, 2025:
- The U.S. defense-industrial base is still dominated at the prime level by the traditional “Big Five” (Lockheed Martin, RTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, Northrop Grumman). Analyses of defense acquisition trends still describe these firms as the core prime contractors capturing a very large share of DoD prime contract obligations, with no clear, formally recognized expansion to “7–10” new primes alongside them yet.【turn1search2】
- Anduril is a fast‑growing defense tech company winning significant Pentagon and allied contracts, including Space Force missile‑defense work and large drone and undersea programs, but it is still described as a “defense startup” or newer defense tech contractor rather than a fully established prime on the scale of the Big Five.【turn0news12】【turn0news13】【turn0search22】
- Epirus has raised substantial funding (over $550M total) and secured notable contracts such as a $66M U.S. Army high‑power microwave deal, yet it remains a venture‑backed defense startup, not a broadly recognized major prime.【turn0news15】【turn0news16】【turn0search18】
- Saronic is likewise a rapidly scaling autonomous‑vessel defense company with large funding rounds and plans for a futuristic shipyard and large unmanned warships; it is covered as an ambitious new defense contractor, not as a peer prime to Lockheed/General Dynamics today.【turn1news12】【turn1search13】【turn1news14】

Because (1) the prediction’s outcome is explicitly tied to a multi‑year/decades horizon, and (2) we are still early in that window, with neither clear evidence that 7–10 new primes *have* emerged nor that they *cannot* emerge over the stated timeframe, the correct assessment as of Nov 30, 2025 is **inconclusive (too early to tell)**.

They are 'neo-primes'/disruptors but not yet major primes.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence since the episode released (Dec 2024) shows:

1. **U.S. “next‑gen” hardware did arrive and is shipping at massive scale.**  
   * NVIDIA’s Blackwell architecture for data‑center AI (GB200/B200/B300 and Blackwell Ultra) was announced in March 2024 and is being adopted by all major U.S. hyperscalers; analysts project millions of Blackwell AI GPUs shipping in 2025, with further upgrades (Rubin) slated for 2026. ([nvidianews.nvidia.com](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-blackwell-platform-arrives-to-power-a-new-era-of-computing?utm_source=openai))  
   * AMD has rolled out the Instinct MI325X in late 2024, with MI350‑series accelerators (CDNA 4, 3nm) becoming available in 2025 and MI400 planned for 2026, on an explicit annual high‑end AI roadmap. ([amd.com](https://www.amd.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-10-10-amd-delivers-leadership-ai-performance-with-amd-in.html?utm_source=openai))  
   * Broadcom continues to co‑design and manufacture Google’s TPU accelerators, and by late 2025 Google is negotiating to sell these AI chips more broadly (e.g., to Meta), further concentrating frontier compute in U.S.–aligned platforms. ([investors.com](https://www.investors.com/news/technology/google-in-talks-ai-chips-meta-nvidia-amd/?utm_source=openai))

2. **China’s direct access to this *U.S.* frontier hardware is heavily constrained, but not zero.**  
   * Successive U.S. export‑control rounds have made advanced Nvidia and AMD data‑center GPUs either banned or license‑controlled for China (A100/H100/H200 and China‑specific H20/H800/A800 variants, and analogous AMD parts), with 2024–25 rules explicitly targeting frontier AI chips. ([usimportdata.com](https://www.usimportdata.com/blogs/us-ai-chip-export-restrictions-2025?utm_source=openai))  
   * Nvidia’s CEO has stated there are *no* ongoing discussions to sell Blackwell to China, while the U.S. simultaneously approved tens of thousands of Blackwell chips for Middle Eastern customers—underscoring that most Blackwell supply goes to the U.S. and close partners, not China. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/trump-weighing-advanced-nvidia-chip-sales-china-bloomberg-news-reports-2025-11-24/?utm_source=openai))  
   * Analysts and U.S. officials generally estimate Chinese domestic AI chips to be **~1–2 generations behind** leading Nvidia parts; a Commerce Department official testified in mid‑2025 that Huawei would likely be limited to at most ~200,000 advanced AI chips in 2025 and that its designs still trail U.S. GPUs by about one to two years. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-says-chinas-huawei-cant-make-more-than-200000-ai-chips-2025-2025-06-12/?utm_source=openai))

3. **China is nonetheless building very large domestic AI compute and using work‑arounds.**  
   * Huawei’s Ascend 910B/910C NPUs, fabricated on SMIC’s 7nm node, are roughly in the A100–H100 class on many metrics (often below H100 but above A100), and Huawei is expected to ship on the order of hundreds of thousands to ~800,000+ units in 2025 for domestic AI clusters. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HiSilicon?utm_source=openai))  
   * Huawei’s CloudMatrix 384 “supernode,” unveiled in 2025, combines 384 Ascend 910C chips into a domestic AI cluster that *system‑level* BF16 performance and memory bandwidth benchmarks show **exceeding Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 rack‑scale system**, albeit with far worse power efficiency. This demonstrates that China can reach very high aggregate compute by scaling more, slightly older chips. ([dev.to](https://dev.to/code_performance/deep-dive-reports-on-leading-topics-in-ai-and-digital-modernity-pdo?utm_source=openai))  
   * Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance are training their top‑end LLMs (e.g., Qwen, Doubao) in Southeast‑Asian data centers using Nvidia H100/A100‑class GPUs hosted outside China, thereby legally sidestepping some U.S. export bans while keeping fine‑tuning and deployment inside China. ([tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/semiconductors/chinas-top-ai-firms-shift-model-training-overseas-to-access-nvidia-gpus?utm_source=openai))

4. **China’s AI systems are still competitive at the model level, despite hardware handicaps.**  
   * Reporting and analyses in 2024–25 note that Chinese labs (Alibaba, Tencent, DeepSeek, etc.) have produced LLMs that are competitive with many Western open‑source models, and that “the question is no longer if China can compete in AI” despite export restrictions—suggesting they have not been knocked out of frontier‑scale AI development. ([time.com](https://time.com/7204164/china-ai-advances-chips/?utm_source=openai))  
   * New Chinese models and toolchains (e.g., DeepSeek’s models with first‑class support for Huawei Ascend/CANN) are explicitly optimized for domestic accelerators to reduce dependence on Nvidia/CUDA, again indicating an active *catch‑up* rather than a collapse in capability. ([tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/deepseek-new-model-supports-huawei-cann?utm_source=openai))

**Why this makes the prediction “ambiguous” rather than clearly right or wrong:**

* Gavin’s claim is that once Blackwell and the next AMD/Broadcom generation roll out (i.e., from 2025 onward), *“it is not going to be possible for [China] to keep up anymore”* at the **leading edge of AI compute**.
* On a **narrow hardware‑access metric**—who can buy and deploy the very latest Nvidia/AMD/Broadcom chips at scale inside their own ecosystem—the U.S. and close allies clearly enjoy a major and widening advantage, while China’s access to hardware like Blackwell is sharply constrained and its domestic chips remain a node or more behind. That reading would make the prediction look broadly **right**. ([nvidianews.nvidia.com](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-blackwell-platform-arrives-to-power-a-new-era-of-computing?utm_source=openai))
* But if “keep up” means **practical AI compute capability sufficient to train and deploy competitive frontier‑level models**, then China *is* still keeping up via:  
  – large‑scale domestic clusters built from slightly older but plentiful Huawei/other chips;  
  – access to offshore Nvidia‑based compute; and  
  – algorithmic and software optimizations to squeeze more out of each chip.  
  On that broader interpretation, the prediction looks **too strong**, because China has not dropped out of frontier AI competition by late 2025. ([tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/semiconductors/chinas-top-ai-firms-shift-model-training-overseas-to-access-nvidia-gpus?utm_source=openai))

Because **“keep up at the leading edge of AI compute capability” is not defined in a way that maps cleanly to measurable, public metrics**, and because current evidence supports *both* (a) a clear U.S. edge in *formal* frontier hardware and (b) China’s continued ability to compete at or near the AI frontier through work‑arounds and domestic scaling, the prediction cannot be judged definitively true or false with the information available as of November 30, 2025. Hence, **“ambiguous.”**

Nvidia Blackwell GPUs began shipping in early 2025 (e.g., HPE Grace Blackwell in Feb 2025, Supermicro volume in Sep 2025, GeForce RTX 50-series in Jan 2025), fulfilling the 'next generation' trigger. AMD released/upgraded MI300X/MI325X/MI350X series in 2025 (e.g., Advancing AI event June 2025), though MI400 is 2026. Broadcom advanced custom AI ASICs/networking (e.g., partnerships with OpenAI/Alphabet), boosting AI revenue to $13B FY2025.

By Dec 2025, US leads leading-edge AI compute: xAI Colossus is the world's largest AI supercomputer; US holds 39.7M H100-equivalents (top AI-dominant country); DOE/Oracle deploying 100k Blackwell chips. TOP500: US 175 systems vs China's 47. 

China lags: Huawei Ascend 910C/950 ~1/3 B200 perf per chip, comparable to H200 at best; massive clusters (e.g., Atlas 950 planned 500k+ NPUs by 2026) scale but trail per-chip. Export bans block Blackwell access; US retains hardware edge ([RAND](https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2025/05/chinas-ai-models-are-closing-the-gap-but-americas-real.html), [SemiAnalysis](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/huawei-ai-cloudmatrix-384-chinas-answer-to-nvidia-gb200-nvl72), [TRG Datacenters](https://www.trgdatacenters.com/resource/the-worlds-top-ai-superpowers-in-2025/)). China excels in total capex/scale but not *leading edge* capability post-2025 releases.

predictions.explanation: Grok 3 was in fact trained on xAI’s Colossus supercomputer at the ~100,000–200,000‑GPU scale (far beyond the ~20–32k‑GPU clusters that previous frontier models used), providing precisely the kind of new high‑compute data point Gavin Baker and Friedberg were talking about. ([rdworldonline.com](https://www.rdworldonline.com/how-xai-turned-a-factory-shell-into-an-ai-colossus-to-power-grok-3-and-beyond/?utm_source=openai))  Multiple analysts explicitly framed Grok 3 as an experiment on scaling laws: Tencent/WallstreetCN’s post‑mortem describes Grok 3’s 100k+ H100 run as showing that pre‑training scaling laws “have not hit a ceiling” and still improve performance, albeit with poor cost‑effectiveness, concluding that “Scaling Law did not hit a wall.” ([longbridge.com](https://longbridge.com/en/news/228929436?utm_source=openai))  Technical explainers and blogs similarly note that Grok 3’s performance gains over Grok 2, given roughly 10x more compute, are largely what standard scaling‑law curves predict—clear improvement but not a dramatic new “generation” jump—indicating continued validity of scaling rather than a breakdown. ([uxtigers.com](https://www.uxtigers.com/post/ux-roundup-20250224?utm_source=openai))  Ethan Mollick characterized Grok 3 as the first release we *know* used an order of magnitude more training compute than GPT‑4‑class models and said it would help test whether the first (pre‑training) scaling law still holds; after the results, he wrote that Grok 3 landed right at expectations, with no need to revise the consensus that more compute still buys more capability. ([ethanbholland.com](https://ethanbholland.com/2025/02/21/x-ai-news-week-ending-02-21-2025/?utm_source=openai))  While some online discussions still debate whether we are near a “wall,” the empirical outcome from Grok 3 is broadly read as evidence that scaling laws remain intact at this larger scale rather than having already failed, which is exactly the kind of resolution Friedberg predicted Grok 3 would provide.

predictions.explanation:
By late February 2025, there was substantial but conflicting evidence about whether Grok 3 had truly become the state‑of‑the‑art general‑purpose LLM relative to OpenAI/Microsoft’s best publicly available frontier models.

**Evidence that supports the prediction**
- xAI launched Grok 3 around February 17–20, 2025, describing it as their new flagship model trained with roughly 10× the compute of Grok 2 and claiming it surpasses OpenAI on benchmarks like AIME (math) and GPQA (PhD‑level science). ([es.wikipedia.org](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grok_%28chatbot%29?utm_source=openai))
- xAI’s published benchmarks and coverage in outlets like Beebom and ZeroHedge report Grok 3 outperforming GPT‑4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Pro, and DeepSeek V3 on AIME 2024, GPQA Science, and LiveCodeBench, and also beating OpenAI’s o3‑mini on some reasoning benchmarks. ([beebom.com](https://beebom.com/elon-musk-unveils-grok-3-reasoning-model-beats-o3-mini-deepseek-r1/?utm_source=openai))
- Grok 3 (under the alias “chocolate”) reached the #1 position on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena with an Elo score around 1400–1402, ahead of GPT‑4o and DeepSeek R1, which xAI and supporters framed as evidence it was the top chatbot overall. ([twitter.com](https://twitter.com/i/grok/share/SDCC3U72SkIJb2KXs3ihL1cim?utm_source=openai))

**Evidence that cuts against the prediction**
- Independent commentary after launch emphasized that Grok 3 was *competitive* but not clearly dominant. Ethan Mollick (Wharton) described Grok 3 as a “very solid frontier model” but **not** a clear leader and “not one you would stop using your current frontier model for,” adding that while it beats some OpenAI models on selected benchmarks, it does not clearly surpass OpenAI’s o3. ([aol.com](https://www.aol.com/elon-musks-grok-3-model-135743065.html?utm_source=openai))
- Gary Marcus similarly argued that Elon Musk’s promise that Grok 3 would be “the smartest AI ever” was not borne out, calling the launch “no game changer” relative to OpenAI’s best models. ([aol.com](https://www.aol.com/elon-musks-grok-3-model-135743065.html?utm_source=openai))
- Comparative write‑ups on Grok 3 vs. OpenAI’s o3 report a mixed picture: Grok 3 slightly leads on some math benchmarks (e.g., AIME 2025 under heavy consensus sampling), while o3 (and related OpenAI reasoning models) lead on others, such as Codeforces coding Elo and certain software‑engineering tasks. These articles also note concerns that xAI’s benchmark setups (e.g., very expensive consensus sampling for Grok 3) aren’t perfectly comparable to how OpenAI models are typically evaluated, making it hard to declare an overall winner. ([portotheme.com](https://www.portotheme.com/grok-3-vs-o3-a-comprehensive-comparison/?utm_source=openai))

**Why this is rated ambiguous**
The prediction effectively claims that **by January/February 2025** Grok 3 would *surpass* OpenAI/Microsoft’s best publicly available frontier model and be the **state‑of‑the‑art general‑purpose LLM**. By late February 2025, Grok 3:
- Was clearly a top‑tier frontier model and #1 on one prominent user‑preference leaderboard (Chatbot Arena). ([twitter.com](https://twitter.com/i/grok/share/SDCC3U72SkIJb2KXs3ihL1cim?utm_source=openai))
- But faced credible, well‑publicized expert assessments and technical comparisons saying it **did not clearly surpass** OpenAI’s leading models overall.

Because “state‑of‑the‑art general‑purpose LLM” is not defined by a single universally accepted metric, and high‑quality sources disagree—some framing Grok 3 as SOTA and others explicitly saying OpenAI remained ahead or at least not clearly behind—the outcome of the prediction cannot be determined in a definitive, objective way. Hence the result is best characterized as **ambiguous**, rather than clearly right or clearly wrong.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction is about the *future* ("in 2 or 3 years" from a December 7, 2024 podcast, i.e., roughly 2026–2027). As of today (November 30, 2025), those years have not yet occurred, so we cannot definitively say whether a single top-tier frontier AI model will cost on the order of US$100 billion to train.

Public reporting to date on frontier model training costs (e.g., estimates for models like GPT‑4 and successor projects) generally puts total *training* expenditures in the range of hundreds of millions to low single-digit billions of dollars per model—not anywhere near $100 billion yet. These figures are based on industry analyses and journalistic estimates of GPU usage, cloud spending, and datacenter investments, and even very large announced AI infrastructure projects (e.g., multi‑tens‑of‑billions datacenters) are spread across multiple years and many models, not a single training run. However, these current numbers do not resolve whether *by 2026–2027* costs for a single state‑of‑the‑art model will reach ~$100B.

Because the time window for the prediction has not arrived and the cost level it refers to has not yet been (dis)proven by events in those years, the correct classification is: it is too early to tell.
predictions.grok_explanation: The prediction targets 2026–2027, but current date is Dec 2025, so too early to verify. Current frontier model training costs remain under $200M (e.g., Google Gemini 1.0 Ultra ~$192M per 2025 AI Index/Visual Capitalist; GPT-4 ~$78M). Projections suggest $1B+ by 2027 (Epoch AI, Jun 2024) and $10B–$100B ambitions (Anthropic CEO Amodei, Nov 2024), but no $100B model trained yet. Sources: Epoch AI, arXiv 2405.21015, Visual Capitalist Apr 2025, Stanford AI Index 2025.

predictions.explanation:
By late November 2025 we *do* have powerful "vibe coding" and AI app-builder tools (Lovable, Base44, Bolt.new, Replit, GitHub Spark, Div-idy, etc.) that let users describe apps in natural language and get working full‑stack web apps scaffolded quickly, often including hosting and basic auth.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base44?utm_source=openai))  However, these systems are interactive assistants, not fire‑and‑forget agents: users still iterate prompts, tweak designs, and debug issues rather than simply returning a few hours later to a finished, reliable product.

Independent reviews and user reports consistently say that AI‑generated apps are good for MVPs and small internal tools but are *not* reliably "production‑ready" without additional engineering work—citing brittle code, poor error handling, scaling problems, UX issues, and significant technical debt.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovable?utm_source=openai))  Even Lovable’s own marketing around "production‑ready" code is tempered by community discussions where people bring in developers to harden security, performance, and edge cases before real production use.([claude.com](https://www.claude.com/customers/lovable?utm_source=openai))  Security analyses similarly find that a large fraction of AI‑generated code contains vulnerabilities, and experts explicitly warn that using vibe‑coded software to go from zero to production without disciplined engineering is unsafe.([itpro.com](https://www.itpro.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/vibe-coding-security-risks-how-to-mitigate?utm_source=openai))

Research and surveys on vibe coding describe it as *collaborative*, with humans validating behavior via tests and usage, not as a fully autonomous pipeline where AI handles its own QA and UX iteration end‑to‑end.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibe_coding?utm_source=openai))  Meanwhile, the most advanced autonomous coding agents (e.g., Devin) can plan, run tests, and make multi‑step changes, but independent evaluations show low success rates on realistic tasks and recommend treating them like junior developers whose work must still be reviewed and governed before deployment—far from a system you can safely let design, test, and deploy a new production app unattended.([aiaaic.org](https://www.aiaaic.org/aiaaic-repository/ai-algorithmic-and-automation-incidents/study-devin-ai-software-engineer-fails-at-most-tasks?utm_source=openai))

Because no broadly available tool today lets ordinary end users casually specify an arbitrary app in natural language and have AI autonomously handle architecture, QA, UX design/iteration, and production deployment in a few hours with only minimal human oversight at acceptable reliability, the prediction—as stated—is not borne out within the promised ~12‑month window.

predictions.grok_explanation: By December 2025, tools like Replit Agent 3, Chef by Convex, and Lovable enable end users to describe apps in natural language, autonomously generating full-stack code, performing QA/testing/debugging (e.g., Replit: 'Agent tests its own work... fixes issues it finds'), iterating UX via agent modes or feedback, and deploying production-ready apps (e.g., Convex hosting, Replit deployments) in hours with minimal intervention. Examples: Replit builds 'production-ready Apps' in ~200 min; Chef creates 'complete, production-ready web applications from a single natural language prompt'; Reddit user built '12 production apps... in a couple hours'. Sources: [replit.com](https://replit.com/), [chef.convex.dev](https://chef.convex.dev/), [lovable.dev](https://lovable.dev/), Medium/Reddit reviews (Oct-Nov 2025). While some limitations exist (e.g., prompt quality affects results, not for ultra-complex apps), capabilities match the prediction.

predictions.explanation: As of late 2025, surveys and industry data show that natural‑language prompting is a widely used assistant, not the primary interface for most developers, so Friedberg’s claim that “human language will be the dominant programming language” in 2025 has not materialized. Stack Overflow’s 2025 Developer Survey reports that 84% of respondents use or plan to use AI tools, but many use them only occasionally, 46% explicitly distrust AI output, and about three‑quarters still prefer asking human colleagues over AI for help, indicating that AI (and thus natural‑language prompts) is supplementary rather than central. ([techradar.com](https://www.techradar.com/pro/developers-are-finding-it-hard-to-trust-ai-and-not-just-because-it-could-steal-their-jobs?utm_source=openai)) Studies of GitHub Copilot and large enterprise deployments find that roughly 20–33% of accepted code lines come from AI and that even at Microsoft, AI contributes only around 30% of code in some projects—meaning most code is still written and edited directly in conventional languages like Python and JavaScript. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15033?utm_source=openai)) While 2025 has seen the rise of “vibe coding” and rhetoric that human language is becoming a new kind of programming language, these are consistently described as emerging trends, used mainly for prototyping or specific workflows, and accompanied by significant concerns around security and reliability, not as the default way the majority of professional software is produced. ([rollingai.news](https://rollingai.news/2025/06/09/human-is-the-new-programming-language-per-nvdia-ceo-jensen-huang-on-ai-powered-coding/?utm_source=openai)) Some industry analyses claim that around 41% of global code in 2024 was AI‑generated and that a large share of vibe‑coding users are non‑developers, but even these optimistic estimates imply that most code is still authored through traditional programming and apply to subsets of teams rather than “most developers” worldwide. ([secondtalent.com](https://www.secondtalent.com/resources/vibe-coding-statistics/?utm_source=openai)) Overall, natural‑language interfaces have become important and fast‑growing in 2025, but the best available evidence shows they augment rather than replace conventional programming languages, so the prediction is best judged as wrong.

predictions.grok_explanation: The prediction that natural human language would become the primary interface for most developers (and many non-developers) by sometime in 2025, making it the dominant programming language in practice, has not materialized. Major 2025 surveys show high AI tool adoption (e.g., [Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai): 84% use/planning AI tools, 47% daily; [JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem 2025](https://blog.jetbrains.com/research/2025/10/state-of-developer-ecosystem-2025/): 85% regular use), but these are assistants like GitHub Copilot (67.9% usage) for code generation, autocompletion, boilerplate, and docs—not primary natural language prompting. Crucially, only 16.9% use AI *mostly* for writing code (59% partially); 72% reject 'vibe coding' (pure LLM prompts) as part of work. Developers edit/verify code in IDEs (e.g., VS Code 75.9% usage). Top languages remain JavaScript (66%), Python (57.9%), etc.—no English/natural language listed ([Stack Overflow](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/), [GitHub Octoverse 2025](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-a-new-developer-joins-github-every-second-as-ai-leads-typescript-to-1/): TypeScript #1). Trust is low (46% distrust AI accuracy). No data supports non-developer dominance. Sources confirm AI supplements, not supplants, traditional coding.

This prediction is about what the *global* energy mix and relative costs of solar vs. nuclear and coal will look like roughly 50 years after the Dec 7, 2024 recording date—i.e., around 2074. As of today (late 2025), only about 1 year has passed, so there is nowhere near enough elapsed time to evaluate whether:

- “A lot of the world will run on solar” (i.e., solar becomes the dominant global energy source), and
- Solar power costs end up approaching coal while remaining more expensive than nuclear.

These are long‑horizon structural claims about the 2070s, not near‑term forecasts. Because the target timeframe has not arrived, the prediction cannot yet be judged as right or wrong.

Therefore, the appropriate status is: it is **too early to tell** whether this prediction will come true.
